content.text: Fitting a scaler, imputer or feature selector on the whole dataset before splitting lets the test rows help build the model. For a plain scaler the damage is often invisible; for a step that reads the labels it's huge: 0.777 accuracy on coin-flip labels. Put every step that learns from data in a

A research team predicts a disease from 5,000 gene readings per patient, with 300 patients. Following a tutorial, they standardize the data, keep the 20 genes most associated with the diagnosis, and cross-validate a logistic regression: 0.777 accuracy. A reviewer asks for the code, moves the same two steps inside the cross-validation, and gets 0.503. The model was never better than a coin flip. Every step was standard; the order was the bug.
Many developers believe preprocessing on the full dataset is harmless, as long as the model itself is trained only on the training split. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: Preprocessing feels like cleaning, not learning. A column's mean and standard deviation don't look like a model.

Often the score really doesn't move. In the script below, scaling the whole dataset first changes nothing at all.

content.text: The half-truth: for a scaler on hundreds of rows, the leaked statistics are close to what the training rows alone would give. But "preprocess everything, then split" is a code structure, and not every step that goes through it is a scaler.
scikit-learn's guide to common pitfalls defines
as using information that wouldn't be available at prediction time while building the model. Its rule is short: never call
estimates numbers from the rows it sees.
learns each column's mean and spread,
learns which columns are most related to
. In production, none of those numbers can come from tomorrow's requests. If they come from your test rows during evaluation, the evaluation describes a model you can't deploy.
What leaks depends on what the step reads

Unsupervised steps, such as scalers, imputers and PCA, read the test rows' features but not their labels. The effect is usually small, but Moscovich and Rosset show it's a real bias in cross-validation that can push the estimate up or down, depending on the data, the transformation, the model and the sample sizes. You can't even tell which way you're wrong.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 5000))  # 300 patients, 5,000 gene readings
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=300)  # coin-flip labels: nothing to learn

X_all = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)  # fitted on every row
X_all = SelectKBest(k=20).fit_transform(X_all, y)  # reads every label
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_all, y, cv=5)
print(f"accuracy {scores.mean():.3f}")
# accuracy 0.777

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 5000))
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=300)

pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectKBest(k=20),
                     LogisticRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)  # every step refit per fold
print(f"all steps in the pipeline: accuracy {scores.mean():.3f}")

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)  # only the scaler outside
pipe = make_pipeline(SelectKBest(k=20), LogisticRegression())
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X_scaled, y, cv=5)
print(f"scaler fitted on all rows: accuracy {scores.mean():.3f}")
# all steps in the pipeline: accuracy 0.503
# scaler fitted on all rows: accuracy 0.503

content.text: ranked 5,000 random columns by how well they matched all 300 labels. Out of 5,000, some 20 match by pure chance, including on the rows each fold later uses for validation. The model then "predicts" labels that picked its own features, and reports 0.777 for nothing. scikit-learn's pitfalls guide shows the same effect with 10,000 random features: 0.76 instead of 0.5.

The right version reports 0.503. Its last two lines also show why the habit survives: with only the scaler fitted on all rows, the score is identical, 0.503. The scaler alone looked harmless here, so nobody questioned the structure that let the selector leak.
A pipeline makes each fold refit everything
chains the steps into one estimator. Pass it to

with the raw data, and every fold fits a fresh copy: each transformer learns from that fold's training rows only, then transforms the validation rows with what it learned. The scikit-learn guide lists this as the pipeline's safety purpose: it avoids leaking test statistics into the trained model by training the transformers and the predictor on the same samples.
You get two more things for free.
can tune preprocessing and model together, with names like
. And the fitted pipeline carries its scaler and imputer into production, so new rows get exactly the training-time transformation.
It isn't only a beginner's mistake

Kapoor and Narayanan surveyed leakage across fields that adopted machine learning and found errors in 17 fields, affecting 329 papers. Preprocessing on training and test data together, and feature selection on both, are two of the eight leakage types in their taxonomy. In their civil war prediction case study, one paper imputed its training and out-of-sample test data together while more than 95% of the test values were missing. Corrected, its random forest did no better than logistic regression.

blocks.title: A pipeline only guards what's inside it

content.text: Choices you make by eye leak too: picking columns from a correlation plot of the full dataset, dropping outliers by full-data percentiles, or tuning a cutoff in a notebook. The pipeline can't see those decisions, so make them on training data only, or turn them into pipeline steps.
